description: I’m into Earth observation and data analysis, working mainly in Python (pandas, numpy, plotly, Streamlit). I’m building a web app with a harmonized burning activity calendar from 2000 to today, based on NASA FIRMS data, for emergency responders, land managers and scientists.
summary: Seamless Fire is a burning activity calendar for any area, from 2000 to today, on one consistent scale. MODIS (from 2000) and VIIRS (from 2012) see fire differently, so joining their records creates a false jump in 2012. We harmonize them with a per-country, per-season model, validated year by year on the years both sensors flew, and we remove industrial heat sources that would otherwise make up three quarters of Polish VIIRS "fires". Emergency managers, land managers and firefighters pick a country, a preset, a rectangle or a polygon drawn on the map, and see which months and years burned most, how the current month compares with the same days in earlier years, long-term trends, and where fires return year after year at ~1 km. A 7-day fire weather outlook ranks the places to watch, each named by the nearest town. Recent days come from NASA FIRMS near real-time data; everything downloads as CSV with a column guide and the area outline, or as a one-file area report.
details:
What it does. Seamless Fire shows the fire history of any area as a calendar heatmap (years × months) from January 2000 to today, on one consistent scale, for Poland, Portugal, Spain, Greece, Ukraine, Australia, Canada and Chile. Users pick a country, a preset (e.g. Biebrza valley, Algarve), a rectangle or a polygon drawn on the map, and a date range. The app answers:

  • Which months and years burned most? Calendar, per-year chart with uncertainty, and the top 10 anomalies (months most above their usual level). Estimated values always come with their ~80% range.
  • Which fires were largest? Months with very dense detections are flagged as large-fire months: Evia and Evros in Greece, Pedrógão in Portugal, Black Summer in Australia.
  • How does now compare with the past? The "Now" panel compares the current month so far with the same days in earlier years. "This season" compares activity since 1 January with the usual range.
  • Is it changing? Theil–Sen trends with a Mann–Kendall test. Burning declines by 3–4% per year in all five European countries. In Podkarpacie, spring grass burning declines by 5.5% per year, seen by both sensors independently.
  • Where? Fire cells and exact hotspots on the map, and a ~1 km recurrence map that shows where fire returns year after year, with likely industrial sites marked.
  • What comes next? A 7-day outlook from the Canadian Fire Weather Index (NASA POWER history, Open-Meteo forecasts), with skill measured on archived forecasts (Portugal: 32% better than the seasonal normal on day 1). "Places to watch" ranks recurrent fire spots by the coming fire weather, each named by the nearest town.
  • Downloads: CSV of the monthly series and hotspots (with README and area outline as GeoJSON), and a one-file HTML area report.

How it works.

  1. Unit. VIIRS (375 m) splits one fire into several detections, MODIS (1 km) does not, so raw counts are not comparable. We count cell-days: 0.1° cells with at least one detection on a day.
  2. Industrial filter. Only FIRMS vegetation detections (type 0) are kept. Without this, 72% of Polish VIIRS "fires" would be steelworks, refineries and gas flares.
  3. Harmonization. Per country: log(1 + VIIRS) = a[season] + b · log(1 + MODIS), calibrated on 2012–2025. Of five methods compared by leave-one-year-out validation, this one has the lowest error in every country, often half that of simple ratios. Raw counts jump ×1.7–3.5 in 2012; the harmonized series does not (2012/2011 ratio 0.85–1.12). The 2000–2011 interval comes from validation errors plus the sensor drift measured in a backtest.
  4. Custom areas. The browser sums raw cell-days inside the area, then applies the model. Before 2012 an area gets its share of the country estimate, with a wider interval.
  5. Today. One script fetches the FIRMS NOAA-20 near real-time feed, assigns points to countries, removes industrial cells and redeploys the site. NOAA-20 is put on the S-NPP scale with a per-country factor.

Benefits. One consistent 26-year record instead of two incompatible ones. Honest uncertainty where the record is estimated. Today's activity in historical context. 1 km detail for planning patrols and prevention, with industrial sites told apart from vegetation fires.

Tools. Python (pandas, numpy) computes the data; a static Astro site with TypeScript, Plotly and Leaflet displays it, hosted on GitHub Pages. The browser harmonization is tested against the Python reference.

Limitations. Cell-days measure how widespread fire activity was, not burned area. Very large fires saturate them, which is why large-fire months are flagged from VIIRS detections. 2000–2011 values are estimates with intervals, and near real-time data are preliminary. All evidence: docs/validation.md in the repository.
